Vespa Mode’s Implementation and Optimization

Vespa Mode chose not to use the full, complicated Water plugin and instead preferred a highly optimized custom material applied to a simple plane. The infamous unpredictability of water physics makes it challenging to replicate. The optimized version employs subtle consistencies that mimic the essential characteristics of real water physics. For Vespa Mode specifically, this involved utilizing multiple integrations related to UV-animated coordinates in UE5’s blueprints. The implementation and optimization will be categorized with the foundational technique of layered panning, the scale-independent tiling, and the complementary enhancements.

  ***i.***	    The foundational technique of layered panning as it relates to Vespa Mode’s implementation and optimization.

| ----- |
| Figure 1: [Animating UV Coordinates in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.6 Documentation | Epic Developer Community](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/animating-uv-coordinates-in-unreal-engine) |

| ![][image2] |

| Figure 2: “[PanningUVs.mp4 \- Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1I_gZo3pSqy1AdlWrGoARPFcwR3VNXjJv/view)” |

For optimization and layering, the “Animating UV Coordinates” documentation suggests stacking multiple panned textures at different speeds and directions to create more complex and less repetitive motion, a fundamental for optimization and visual quality. Refer to Figure 1\. Vespa Mode followed the documentation’s advice on laying but implemented it practically. They created two identical networks of texture-panner setups and added the outputs together. By setting the two layers to pan at different speeds and in different directions, they broke up the predictable and repetitive pattern of a single panned texture. This, like the documentation suggests, creates a much more complex and believable water surface with minimal performance costs, directly combating the “tiling” artifact mentioned in the UV documentation. See Figure 2 for how this was implemented in Vespa Mode. 

  ***ii.***	    The scale independent tiling technique as it relates to Vespa Mode’s implementation and optimization

| ![][image3] |
| ----- |
| Figure 3: “[PanningUVs.mp4 \- Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1I_gZo3pSqy1AdlWrGoARPFcwR3VNXjJv/view)” |

So there is a problem when scaling a plane in the world (e.g., to make a large ocean): the UVs stretch, making the water waves look artificially large. The default behavior is to resize the entire texture across the object. Vespa's solution is to dynamically link the material’s tiling to the object’s world scale. They did this by taking the object’s scale (from an Object Position or similar node, masked to the X and Y axes) and multiplying this scale value with the TextureCoordinate node’s output before it feeds into the Panner. This ensures that when you make the plane larger, the material automatically tiles the texture more to cover the increased surface area, keeping the perceived wave size consistent. This is the “quality of life” feature Vespa Mode highlighted, as it allows for rapid world-building without manually adjusting materials for every scaled water plane. It effectively makes the water material “procedural” in its response to object size. 

  ***iii.***	    The complementary enhancements technique as it relates to Vespa Mode’s implementation and optimization

Their geometry choice Vespa Mode is used with a plane instead of a cube or any other complex mesh. This is optimization, as it drastically reduces the triangle count for large surfaces. The material property as it relates to Vespa Mode is setting the material’s Blend Mode to Translucent and the adjusted Opacity, which is crucial for seeing through to the riverbed or ocean floor; this adds realism without having to do the heavy physics-based solution required in the Water System plugin.
